_meta.title: BGP route visibility and path analysis runbook - Topolograph
_meta.description: Load the Topolograph BGP demo, inspect BMP sessions and routes, understand RIB visibility, and verify BGP best-path decisions and next-hop resolution.
_meta.meta_keywords: BGP visualization, BMP RFC 7854, BMP RFC 8671, BMP RFC 9069, BGP best path, BGP route reflector
_meta.og_title: BGP route visibility and path analysis runbook
_meta.og_description: A practical Topolograph runbook for BGP sessions, RIB visibility, best-path decisions, and BGP next-hop resolution over OSPF.

page_title: BGP route visibility and path analysis
page_intro: Use the built-in demo to inspect the route view Topolograph can prove, verify a best-path decision, compare route state over time, and follow a BGP next hop through OSPF.
nav_node_card: Route view in the device form
demo_intro: The generated BGP demo loads automatically. It contains 13 routers, 22 BGP sessions, and two route reflectors with deliberately different BMP capabilities.
demo_steps: Confirm that the generated demo topology is present; no upload or manual demo load is required.
Open General View and confirm that the BGP overlay is visible. The overlay is enabled by default; the control can hide and restore it.

Find the routers with Router IDs 123.123.100.100 (RFC 7854) and 123.123.101.101 (RFC 7854 + RFC 9069 + RFC 8671). These RFCs identify which RIBs Topolograph receives through BMP from each route reflector.
demo_result: The IGP topology remains the base graph. The BGP overlay adds sessions without replacing OSPF connectivity.
sessions_intro: Use both representations: the table provides precise BGP-session filtering, while the graphical BGP-session overlay shows where the selected session sits in the topology.
sessions_steps: Open BGP Sessions and filter the peer ip column by 123.123.31.31.
Confirm that 123.123.31.31 (PE31) has one BGP session, with 123.123.100.100 (RR1), and no BGP session with 123.123.101.101 (RR2).
Return to General View and locate the same PE-to-123.123.100.100 (RR1) adjacency in the BGP overlay.
sessions_visual: The filtered BGP Sessions table below makes the RFC 7854 limitation case concrete: 123.123.31.31 (PE31) has one observed session, to 123.123.100.100 (RR1).
sessions_alt: BGP Sessions table filtered for 123.123.31.31 (PE31), showing its only session to 123.123.100.100 (RR1)
sessions_result: This 123.123.31.31 (PE31), with one BGP session, demonstrates the RFC 7854 limitation used later in the runbook.
visibility_intro: A BMP session established with a route reflector does not automatically provide a view of every RR client's table. A BMP session capable of exporting Loc-RIB provides the most accurate view of routing-table state. Topolograph can also work with explicit assumptions when some information is unavailable. For example, a device's RIB state can be inferred from a neighboring BMP speaker's RFC 8671 Adj-RIB-Out post-policy toward that device, even when no BMP session is established with the device itself.
rfc_table_title: BMP RFC coverage and path-calculation meaning
rfc_headers: Owner and direction of the observed RIB
Can a path be calculated for the named device?
rfc_rows: Adj-RIB-In belongs to the BMP speaker and contains routes it received from a BGP neighbor
Adj-RIB-In does not show which route the BMP speaker selected and installed in Loc-RIB
Loc-RIB belongs to the BMP speaker and contains its selected routes
Adj-RIB-Out belongs to the BMP speaker and contains routes it advertised to a specific BGP neighbor; for that neighbor, the feed is used as inferred Adj-RIB-In
The BGP neighbor's inbound policy and resulting Loc-RIB are not observed
router_table_title: Routers in the demo network and routing-information visibility
router_rows: Loc-RIB belongs to 123.123.101.101 (RR2) and is received directly from it through RFC 9069
Adj-RIB-Out post-policy belongs to 123.123.101.101 (RR2) and is directed to the corresponding device; for that device it is used as inferred Adj-RIB-In
The device's inbound policy and resulting Loc-RIB are not observed
Adj-RIB-Out post-policy belongs to 123.123.101.101 (RR2) and is directed to the corresponding device; for that device it is used as inferred Adj-RIB-In
The device's inbound policy and resulting Loc-RIB are not observed
The observed Loc-RIB belongs to 123.123.101.101 (RR2); its Adj-RIB-Out toward 123.15.15.15 (PE15) is not exported through BMP
123.123.101.101 (RR2) is assumed to advertise its selected route to 123.15.15.15 (PE15), and 123.15.15.15 (PE15) is assumed to accept it after inbound policy
The observed Loc-RIB belongs to 123.123.101.101 (RR2); its Adj-RIB-Out toward these devices is not exported through BMP
123.123.101.101 (RR2) is assumed to advertise its selected route to each device, and each device is assumed to accept it after inbound policy
RFC 7854 from 123.123.100.100 (RR1) shows its Adj-RIB-In, not its Loc-RIB; path calculation uses the Loc-RIB owned by 123.123.101.101 (RR2), whose Adj-RIB-Out toward RR1 is not exported through BMP
123.123.101.101 (RR2) is assumed to advertise its selected route to 123.123.100.100 (RR1), and 123.123.100.100 (RR1) is assumed to accept it after inbound policy

Adj-RIB-In pre-policy and post-policy belongs to 123.123.100.100 (RR1) and contains routes it received from 123.123.31.31 (PE31); for PE31 this proves only its Adj-RIB-Out. No route data toward PE31 is available
The observed data shows neither the Loc-RIB nor Adj-RIB-In of 123.123.31.31 (PE31)
selective_export_note: 123.123.101.101 (RR2) exports Adj-RIB-Out post-policy data through BMP only for selected BGP neighbors. This is valid: BMP Adj-RIB-Out monitoring is configured per BGP neighbor and address family, even though BGP itself maintains an Adj-RIB-Out for every established BGP neighbor.
all_routes_intro: Start from the graph-wide BGP Routes table before narrowing to one router. This is the place to inspect and filter the route data collected for the whole demo.
all_routes_steps: Open Graph table and select BGP Routes. Leave the table in Live mode.
Use prefix, bmp source, bmp ribs, peer ip, and path-attribute columns to find the route set you want to investigate.
all_routes_visual: The full-screen Live table below is the graph-wide BGP Routes view.
all_routes_alt: Full-screen graph-wide BGP Routes table in Live mode
all_routes_result: The BGP Routes table shows routes collected for the entire graph.
node_card_title: 5. Route view in the device form
node_card_intro: The route count in the device form shows the RIB view for that router: either its Loc-RIB received through a BMP session with the device, or Adj-RIB-Out post-policy received through a BMP session with a neighboring device.
node_card_steps: Click 123.14.14.14 (PE14) on the graph and find the BGP section in the device form.
Confirm Routes is 4 and read the explanation: the routes were advertised by 123.123.101.101 (RR2) to this router through RFC 8671.
Read the RIB breakdown. Adj-RIB-Out post-policy describes 123.123.101.101 (RR2)'s exported RIB; from 123.14.14.14 (PE14)'s perspective these four advertisements are its inferred Adj-RIB-In.

The Adj-RIB-Out (post) 4 row is included in Routes: it is 123.123.101.101 (RR2)'s Adj-RIB-Out toward 123.14.14.14 (PE14), used as 123.14.14.14 (PE14)'s inferred Adj-RIB-In. A separate Advertised (Adj-RIB-Out) counter, when shown, refers to routes that 123.14.14.14 (PE14) itself sent to BGP neighbors and is not included in Routes.
node_card_alt: 123.14.14.14 (PE14) device form showing four routes advertised by 123.123.101.101 (RR2) and Adj-RIB-Out post-policy data
node_card_visual: This form shows the RIB view for 123.14.14.14 (PE14): four routes from Adj-RIB-Out post-policy received through BMP from 123.123.101.101 (RR2).
node_card_result: The device form for 123.14.14.14 (PE14) shows four routes, BMP source 123.123.101.101 (RR2), and RIB Adj-RIB-Out post-policy. Routes does not include routes that 123.14.14.14 (PE14) advertised to 123.123.101.101 (RR2) or other BMP observations not used for 123.14.14.14 (PE14)'s RIB view.
routes_title: 6. Filtering, sorting, and pagination for one node's routes
routes_intro: Open the route table from the device form; the table retains the RIB scope selected for 123.14.14.14 (PE14).
routes_steps: Filter prefix by 100.30.0.0/24. Matching rows and the table counter must both fall from 4 to 1.
Clear the prefix filter and inspect other attributes independently: local pref = 250 leaves two VPN routes, afi = 2 leaves two IPv6 routes, and med = 20 leaves two routes from 123.123.30.30 (PE30).
Clear filters and confirm all four 123.14.14.14 (PE14) routes return. Clearing a table filter must not remove the device scope established by the form.
Click a sortable heading such as prefix, nexthop, local pref, or med. Repeated clicks cycle ascending, descending, and unsorted; address columns use address order, not text order.
Use Rows per page for large route tables. The demo has only one page in this node-scoped example, so the previous and next controls correctly remain disabled.
routes_alt: 123.14.14.14 (PE14) route table filtered from four routes to the prefix 100.30.0.0/24
routes_visual: The table below retains the 123.14.14.14 (PE14) scope and adds the prefix filter, leaving one matching route.
routes_result: The filtered row shows 123.123.101.101 (RR2) as bmp source and Adj-RIB-Out post-policy as the observed RIB.
best_path_intro: For each prefix, the demo demonstrates one best-path selection criterion. Start with AS_PATH: compare the candidate attributes, then build the route from 123.123.101.101 (RR2) and verify the selected BGP next hop.
as_path_steps: Compare the two candidates: both have Local Preference 100, Origin IGP, and MED 10. 123.123.30.30 (PE30) advertises AS_PATH 65010 65011 65012; 123.14.14.14 (PE14) advertises AS_PATH 65010.
Switch to BGP / VPN path mode. Set Router to 123.123.101.101 (RR2), VPN or global table to global, and To to 198.18.2.0/24; then select Build a path.
In Route resolution, confirm the first row is BGP on 123.123.101.101 (RR2) with next hop 123.14.14.14 (PE14). The remaining rows resolve that selected next hop through IGP.
as_path_candidates_alt: BGP route filters and the two AS_PATH candidates for 198.18.2.0/24
as_path_builder_alt: BGP VPN path form set to 123.123.101.101 (RR2), the global table, and 198.18.2.0/24
as_path_builder_visual: Next, select the BGP / VPN path form and enter 123.123.101.101 (RR2), the global table, and this prefix.
as_path_result_alt: Route resolution showing 123.123.101.101 (RR2)'s BGP decision with 123.14.14.14 (PE14) as the selected next hop
as_path_resolution_visual: In Route resolution, the first row shows 123.123.101.101 (RR2) selecting 123.14.14.14 (PE14) as the BGP next hop; the following rows are built from OSPF data.
as_path_result: The post-policy candidates differ in AS_PATH length while Local Preference, Origin, and MED tie. Building the route from 123.123.101.101 (RR2) selects 123.14.14.14 (PE14) as the BGP next hop; the following IGP rows show reachability to that BGP next hop.
decision_rows: Lower MED from the same neighboring AS
Different neighboring AS values make MED ineligible
Lower originator ID after earlier ties
advanced_text: The demo shows the six BGP best-path selection criteria listed in the table above. It does not demonstrate selection of eBGP over iBGP, IGP cost to the next hop, route age, cluster-list length, or BGP neighbor address.
compare_intro: Live shows the current route-table state. Compare evaluates route state at T0 and T1.
compare_steps: Open the graph-wide BGP Routes table and switch from Live to Compare.
Keep the default one-hour T0 to T1 window created when the demo loads, then press Run.
The table shows one added route, 100.14.210.0/24; changed at contains the time of its last change before T1.

added means the route is absent at T0 and present at T1; withdrawn means it is present at T0 and absent at T1; changed means it is present at both instants but its attributes differ. Events after T1 are outside the comparison.
Switch back to Live to open the current route-table state.
compare_alt: BGP route Compare mode showing 100.14.210.0/24 as added in the default one-hour window
compare_visual: The comparison below is the endpoint difference for the default demo window, not a chronological event log.
compare_result: For the default demo interval, route 100.14.210.0/24 has status added and MED 80 at T1.
events_intro: Events uses the same BGP Routes drawer and time range, but preserves every route and peer observation instead of reducing them to a T0-to-T1 difference.
events_steps: Switch from Compare to Events and keep a time window that covers the demo change burst.
Press Run and verify one route add, one peer down event, and one route change for 100.14.210.0/24.
Use event, kind, prefix, peer source, peer target, and at to distinguish route changes from BGP-session state changes.
events_visual: The Events view below lists the observations chronologically: the added route, the peer-down event, then the changed route with MED 80.
events_alt: BGP Routes Events mode showing a route add, a peer down event, and a route change
events_result: Events shows all three observations in order. Unlike Compare, it keeps intermediate events even when the final route state is unchanged.
resolution_intro: BGP chooses the route; OSPF supplies reachability to the selected BGP next hop. The path view shows that handoff explicitly.
resolution_steps: In Standard / IGP path mode, use 123.123.30.30 (PE30) as the source and 100.14.0.0/24 as the destination.
Inspect the selected BGP row and identify 123.14.14.14 (PE14) as the BGP next hop.
Open Route resolution and read the result from left to right: the first row is BGP with administrative distance 200 and next hop 123.14.14.14 (PE14).
Continue through the five IGP rows with administrative distance 110 that physically resolve reachability from 123.123.30.30 (PE30) to 123.14.14.14 (PE14).
resolution_alt: Route resolution table with one BGP decision followed by five IGP next-hop-resolution rows
resolution_visual: The table below separates the single BGP route choice from the IGP hops that make its next hop reachable.
resolution_result: The BGP next hop points to 123.14.14.14 (PE14); the rest of the route is then built from OSPF data.
limits_intro: Filter for 123.123.31.31 (PE31). Topolograph can show the routes that 123.123.100.100 (RR1) received from 123.123.31.31 (PE31), but RFC 7854 alone does not reveal which route 123.123.31.31 (PE31) installed or what 123.123.100.100 (RR1) advertised back to it.
limits_steps: Open BGP Routes and filter the peer ip column by 123.123.31.31. Adj-RIB-In (pre) and Adj-RIB-In (post) show routes that 123.123.100.100 (RR1) received from 123.123.31.31 (PE31), not 123.123.31.31 (PE31)'s routing table.
Open the BGP / VPN path form and select Router 123.123.31.31. The form warns that this router's table is not observed and does not allow a path to be built from BGP data.

Compare 123.123.31.31 (PE31) with 123.15.15.15 (PE15): for 123.15.15.15 (PE15), Topolograph uses 123.123.101.101 (RR2) Loc-RIB and explicitly assumes that 123.123.101.101 (RR2) advertised the route to 123.15.15.15 (PE15) and 123.15.15.15 (PE15) applied its inbound policy.
limits_result: Topolograph does not build a path when the available BMP data does not describe the selected device's routing table. To remove this limit, provide the device's Loc-RIB through RFC 9069 or its per-neighbor Adj-RIB-Out post-policy through RFC 8671.
